# Changelog and docs before the PR

Read the workspace's steps in `workit grant show` (`changelog:`, `changelog
file:` and `docs:`).
Both default to `off`: then skip this file. Do them last, on the final diff,
right before `workit pr create`.

## Changelog (`changelog: update|create`)

A PR whose title type is chore, test, docs, ci, build or style (no `!`) needs
no entry. Under `update`, a repo without its changelog file needs none either.
The file is CHANGELOG.md at the root unless `changelog file:` names another
path (or several, one per package: write the entry in the one the change
belongs to). Otherwise:

1. Write one bullet per change a user can see, leading with what they can now
   do, not with internals: "Added: `workit pr create --no-changelog <reason>`
   skips the changelog check with a recorded reason", not "refactor gate
   module".
2. Apply it only with `workit changelog apply --entries '{"Added": ["…"]}'`
   (categories: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security), adding
   `--path <file>` when the file is not the root CHANGELOG.md. It
   merges into `## [Unreleased]` and creates the Keep a Changelog file when it
   is missing. Never clobber CHANGELOG.md: never rewrite, reorder or delete an
   existing entry, and never hand-edit released sections.
3. Commit it (`workit git commit -m "<message>" -- <file>`)
   with the change, then push.

`workit pr create` refuses a user-facing PR without a new Unreleased bullet
(`changelog_required`) and prints the exact `workit changelog apply` command.
When the PR truly needs no entry, pass `--no-changelog "<why>"`: the reason is
written into the PR body.

## Docs (`docs: when-user-facing`)

Only when user-facing behavior changed (same types as above):

1. Read the diff against the base and list each public surface it touches:
   commands, flags, settings, outputs, defaults.
2. Fix only lines the diff makes false in README.md and the guides. Do not
   write new prose for a surface no doc covers: name it under "Docs" in the
   PR body as uncovered instead.
3. A pass that changed nothing is still reported in the PR body: "Docs:
   checked README.md, docs/guides/x.md; nothing the diff made false."

# PR body

Write the body so a reviewer can judge the change fast. This is Workit's
template; when `workit pr template` prints the repo's own, fill that one
instead. Use three sections, in this order, and nothing else the reviewer has
to read.

1. **Summary:** the smallest visual that makes the change clear (pseudocode, a
   call tree, a file tree, a Mermaid diagram or one diff hunk), with a sentence
   or two in the domain's words.
2. **Evidence:** before and after, observed, never asserted. Name the checks
   recorded on the head SHA (`workit ledger list --branch <b> --type check`)
   and the verdict (`workit ledger check --branch <b>`), or a command with its
   output: red before the change, green after.
3. **Merge danger:** one line. One-way door (hard to undo: a migration, a
   published format, a release) or two-way door (a revert undoes it), plus
   the blast radius: who or what breaks if it is wrong (the review skill's
   impact reference lists the surfaces to check).

## Example

```md
## Summary
Ship skill, step 5: "fix CI" → "reproduce with `workit check`, then fix the root cause"

## Evidence
- `check` row: `test` exit 0 on 4be1c2d (`workit ledger list --branch docs/ship-ci --type check`)
- `verdict` row: verified, kind review, non-author session (`workit ledger check --branch docs/ship-ci`)

## Merge danger
Two-way door: skill text only, a revert restores it. Blast radius: agents that babysit PRs, on every host.
```

# Release (git-flow, without the git-flow binary)

"Do the release" means start, commits, finish. Never publish unless asked.

1. `workit release start <version>` (`--hotfix` from production, `--track <t>`
   on a release track). It cuts `release/<version>` locally from develop (or
   the track's integration branch) and never pushes it.
2. Commit the version bump, the changelog section (`## [<version>]`) and the
   docs on it (`workit git commit -m "<msg>" -- <paths>`);
   late fixes go there too. Never commit
   to main or develop directly.
3. `workit release finish --dry-run` shows each step and whether it is done.
   `workit release finish` then merges into production (`--no-ff`), tags
   `<prefix><version>` with the changelog section, merges the tag back into
   develop (and every merge-back branch of the track), deletes the local
   branch, pushes production, develop and the tag atomically, creates the
   GitHub or GitLab release and verifies the tag on the remote. It needs the
   `release` and `push` grants; when blocked, report the grant it names.
   Before it, the release notes (workspace `releaseNotes`, `workit grant
   show` prints it; `off` skips the forge release):
   `workit release notes draft <version>` writes the draft and prints its
   path. Add a `## Highlights` section at its top: 1-3 bullets of what users
   get, from the user's pointers, in their words, not commit subjects.
   Rerunning draft keeps them. Under `review`, finish refuses
   (`release_notes_unapproved`) until the user approves: show the user the
   draft and stop. They run `workit release notes approve <version>` in
   their own terminal; never run it for them. Edit the draft after approval
   only when they ask, then they approve again.
4. Interrupted (a conflict, a failed push, no forge release yet): fix the
   cause and rerun the `resume` command it printed. Steps already done are
   skipped, never repeated.

`workit release publish` pushes the release branch, and is the only verb
that does. Use it only when the user asks (others commit to it, CI must run
on it). Outside git-flow, finish pushes the branch and opens a release PR
into the trunk instead, its body the release notes (draft and approve them
first, as in step 3). Once it merges, tag the merge and run
`workit git push --release <tag>`: it publishes the forge release with the
same notes (under `review`, only the approved draft).
